lessons.title: Cloud Models: Public, Private, Hybrid
concepts: Public cloud: services over the public internet, shared multi-tenant infrastructure, pay-as-you-go (e.g., Azure).
Private cloud: dedicated infrastructure for one organization, on-premises or hosted — maximum control, you manage it.
Hybrid cloud: public + private working together — keep sensitive data on-premises, burst to public cloud for scale.
Exam angle: 'a company wants to keep data on-premises but use cloud for overflow' → hybrid. Always match the model to the requirement.

example.code:
MODEL PICKER:
  Need to burst for seasonal traffic, keep DB local? → Hybrid
  Startup, no datacenter, scale fast? → Public
  Regulator demands dedicated hardware? → Private
example.walkthrough: Draw the three models as overlapping circles. Place five sample workloads — if you hesitate, that is the exam question.

pitfalls: Calling hybrid 'using two public clouds' — that is multicloud, not hybrid.
Thinking private cloud means 'no virtualization' — private clouds are heavily virtualized, just dedicated.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write one-sentence justifications for public vs private vs hybrid for: a bank, a gaming startup, a hospital.

lessons.title: CapEx vs OpEx and the Consumption Model
concepts: CapEx: upfront spending on physical infrastructure — servers you buy, depreciate, and maintain.
OpEx: pay-as-you-go operational spending — Azure bills per second/minute of use; scale down and the bill shrinks.
Consumption-based model: no upfront cost, pay only for what you use, stop paying when you stop using.
Exam angle: 'eliminate upfront hardware costs' → OpEx / consumption model. This is the financial heart of cloud.

example.code:
COST MATH:
  On-prem server: $10k CapEx + $2k/yr power/cooling/staff
  Azure VM: $0 CapEx + ~$150/mo OpEx, deletable anytime
  Break-even thinking is exactly what AZ-900 tests.
example.walkthrough: Explain CapEx vs OpEx to a non-technical friend. If they get it, you own it.

pitfalls: Saying cloud is 'always cheaper' — it is cheaper to START; at steady massive scale, compare carefully.
Forgetting that stopping resources stops billing — the exam loves 'deallocate the VM' cost questions.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: List three costs that disappear when you move a workload from on-premises to Azure pay-as-you-go.

lessons.title: Benefits of Cloud: The Exam List
concepts: High availability: SLA-backed uptime (e.g., 99.9% = ~8.8h downtime/year; 99.99% = ~53min/year).
Scalability vs elasticity: scalability = ability to scale; elasticity = automatic scaling with demand.
Agility: deploy in minutes, not months — no procurement cycles.
Geo-distribution: deploy near users worldwide. Disaster recovery: paired regions, backups, failover.

example.code:
MEMORY ANCHORS:
  99.9% → 'three nines' → 8.76 h/yr downtime
  99.95% → 4.38 h/yr | 99.99% → 52.6 min/yr
  Scalability = CAN scale | Elasticity = DOES scale automatically
example.walkthrough: The exam asks these as definitions and as scenario picks ('needs automatic scale-out' → elasticity).

pitfalls: Mixing scalability and elasticity — the exam distinguishes them deliberately.
Thinking geo-distribution is only about latency — it is also about compliance and DR.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write the downtime math for 99.9%, 99.95%, 99.99% from memory. Check yourself.

lessons.title: Cloud Service Types: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
concepts: IaaS: you manage OS/apps, cloud manages hardware/virtualization (Azure VMs). Most control, most management.
PaaS: cloud manages OS/runtime, you manage code/data (App Service, Azure SQL). Less management, less control.
SaaS: fully managed software you consume (Microsoft 365). Least management, least control.
Shared responsibility shifts with each: IaaS = you patch the OS; PaaS = Microsoft patches; SaaS = you manage users/data only.

example.code:
RESPONSIBILITY LADDER:
  IaaS:  you ── OS, apps, data | cloud ── hardware, virt
  PaaS:  you ── apps, data  | cloud ── + OS, runtime
  SaaS:  you ── data, users | cloud ── everything else
example.walkthrough: Classify 10 Azure services into IaaS/PaaS/SaaS. The exam does exactly this.

pitfalls: Calling Azure SQL 'IaaS' — it is PaaS (managed database). SQL on a VM is IaaS.
Thinking PaaS means 'no configuration' — you still configure scale, networking, and access.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify: Azure VMs, App Service, Microsoft 365, Azure SQL Database, AKS. Answers: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, PaaS, PaaS.

lessons.title: Shared Responsibility Model
concepts: Microsoft always owns: physical datacenter, hosts, network controls — the 'cloud of the cloud'.
You always own: data, endpoints, accounts, access management — the 'in the cloud' part.
IaaS adds to you: OS patching, network config, app security. PaaS/SaaS shift more to Microsoft.
Exam angle: 'who patches the OS on an Azure VM?' → YOU. 'Who secures the physical host?' → Microsoft.

example.code:
ALWAYS-YOU vs ALWAYS-MICROSOFT:
  You: data classification, identity, device security
  Microsoft: physical security, hypervisor patching
  Depends on model: OS, runtime, network controls
example.walkthrough: This is SC-900 territory too — shared responsibility underpins Zero Trust.

pitfalls: Answering 'Microsoft' for data protection — your data is always your responsibility.
Forgetting identity: compromised credentials bypass every Microsoft-owned control.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: For IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: list who patches the OS in each. (You / Microsoft / Microsoft.)

lessons.title: Regions, Availability Zones & Paired Regions
concepts: A region is a set of datacenters in a geographic area (e.g., East US). Choose regions near users and compliant with data residency.
Availability Zones are physically separate datacenters within a region — deploy across zones for 99.99% VM SLA.
Region pairs: each region is paired with another for disaster recovery (e.g., East US ↔ West US); platform updates roll one pair at a time.
Exam angle: 'protect against datacenter failure within a region' → Availability Zones. 'Cross-region DR' → paired regions.

example.code:
RESILIENCE LADDER:
  1 datacenter → single point of failure
  Availability Zones → survive datacenter loss
  Paired regions → survive regional disaster
example.walkthrough: High availability is a design choice, not a default — you must architect across zones.

pitfalls: Thinking one VM is 'highly available' — a single VM SLA is 99.9%; zones get 99.99%.
Confusing zones with regions — zones are within one region.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Name the region pair concept and one example pair. Explain when you would use zones vs pairs.

lessons.title: Compute: VMs, App Service, Containers, Functions
concepts: Azure VMs (IaaS): full control, you manage the OS. Use for lift-and-shift and custom images.
App Service (PaaS): managed web hosting — deploy code, Microsoft manages runtime/OS. Autoscale built in.
Containers: AKS (managed Kubernetes) for orchestration; Container Instances for quick single-container runs.
Azure Functions (serverless): event-driven code, pay per execution — ideal for sporadic workloads.

example.code:
COMPUTE PICKER:
  Need OS control? → VMs
  Web app, minimal mgmt? → App Service
  Microservices at scale? → AKS
  Event-driven, sporadic? → Functions
example.walkthrough: The exam asks 'which compute for X' constantly — memorize this picker.

pitfalls: Using VMs for everything — over-management and over-cost.
Using Functions for long-running jobs — timeouts and cost; use App Service or AKS.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify: lift-and-shift ERP, startup web API, nightly ETL trigger, 50-microservice platform.

lessons.title: Networking: VNets, Subnets, Peering, VPN/ExpressRoute
concepts: Virtual Network (VNet): your isolated network in Azure. Subnets segment it (e.g., web, app, db tiers).
VNet peering connects VNets privately with low latency — no internet traversal.
VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnel over the internet. ExpressRoute: private dedicated connection — more secure, consistent latency, higher cost.
Network Security Groups (NSGs) filter traffic at subnet/NIC level — your virtual firewall rules.

example.code:
CONNECTIVITY LADDER:
  VNet peering → same-cloud private
  VPN Gateway → encrypted over internet
  ExpressRoute → private dedicated circuit
example.walkthrough: Draw a hub-spoke VNet with peering, then add on-premises via ExpressRoute.

pitfalls: Exposing databases directly — always place in private subnets behind NSGs.
Thinking VPN and ExpressRoute are the same — ExpressRoute never touches the public internet.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Design: web tier public, app/db private. Which subnet gets the NSG? (All — defense in depth.)

lessons.title: Storage: Blobs, Files, Disks, Tiers
concepts: Blob Storage: object storage for unstructured data (images, backups). Tiers: Hot, Cool, Archive — cooler = cheaper, slower retrieval.
Azure Files: SMB/NFS file shares in the cloud — lift-and-shift file servers.
Managed Disks: persistent disks for VMs — Premium SSD for I/O-intensive, Standard for cost.
Exam angle: 'rarely accessed, cheapest' → Archive tier. 'VM disk, high IOPS' → Premium SSD.

example.code:
STORAGE PICKER:
  Unstructured + tiers? → Blob (Hot/Cool/Archive)
  File share protocol? → Azure Files
  VM disk? → Managed Disks (match perf tier)
example.walkthrough: Archive tier has hours-long retrieval — never for data you might need quickly.

pitfalls: Putting hot data in Archive — retrieval latency and fees destroy the savings.
One storage account for everything — separate by security/lifecycle needs.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify: nightly DB backups (7yr retention), VM OS disk, shared marketing drive.

lessons.title: Databases: SQL, Cosmos DB, MySQL/PostgreSQL
concepts: Azure SQL Database (PaaS): managed SQL Server — automated backups, patching, scaling. DTU or vCore purchasing.
Cosmos DB: globally distributed NoSQL with single-digit-ms latency and 99.999% SLA — for planet-scale apps.
Azure Database for MySQL/PostgreSQL: managed open-source databases — lift-and-shift without managing servers.
Exam angle: 'global distribution, low latency' → Cosmos DB. 'Relational, managed' → Azure SQL.

example.code:
DATABASE PICKER:
  Relational + managed? → Azure SQL Database
  Global NoSQL + ms latency? → Cosmos DB
  Open-source relational? → MySQL/PostgreSQL PaaS
example.walkthrough: Cosmos DB's killer features: global distribution + multi-model + 99.999% SLA.

pitfalls: Using Cosmos DB for a single-region relational app — overkill and over-cost.
Confusing Azure SQL Database (PaaS) with SQL Server on a VM (IaaS).
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick the database for: global e-commerce cart, lift-and-shift MySQL app, corporate ERP.

lessons.title: Machine Learning: Concepts That Matter
concepts: Supervised learning: train on labeled data (spam/not-spam). Unsupervised: find patterns in unlabeled data (customer segments).
Regression predicts numbers (house prices); classification predicts categories (fraud/legit).
Training vs validation vs test: train learns, validation tunes, test honestly evaluates — never test on training data.
Overfitting: model memorizes training data, fails on new data. Fix: more data, simpler model, regularization.

example.code:
ML VOCAB:
  Label = the answer column | Feature = input column
  Regression → number | Classification → category
  Overfit = memorizes | Underfit = too simple
example.walkthrough: AI-900 loves 'which ML type for X' — spam filter = classification (supervised).

pitfalls: Training on test data — invalidates the evaluation completely.
More complex is better — simplest model that works wins.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify: predict churn (yes/no), forecast sales ($), group customers by behavior.

lessons.title: Computer Vision on Azure
concepts: Image classification: what is in the image (cat/dog). Object detection: what + where (bounding boxes).
OCR: extract text from images (receipts, license plates). Facial services: detection, verification — with Responsible AI limits.
Azure AI Vision provides prebuilt models — no ML expertise needed; call the API.
Custom Vision: train your own classifier with your labeled images when prebuilt is not enough.

example.code:
VISION PICKER:
  What is this? → Image classification
  Where are the defects? → Object detection
  Read this receipt → OCR (Read API)
  Custom categories → Custom Vision
example.walkthrough: Face API has restricted access — Microsoft gates facial recognition behind approval (Responsible AI).

pitfalls: Using object detection when classification suffices — complexity without benefit.
Ignoring Responsible AI limits on facial tech — exam and ethics both test this.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick the service: count cars in a lot, read serial numbers, verify employee badge photo.

lessons.title: Natural Language Processing on Azure
concepts: Language service: sentiment analysis, key phrase extraction, entity recognition, language detection.
Translator: real-time text translation across 100+ languages.
Speech: speech-to-text, text-to-speech, real-time transcription and translation.
Azure OpenAI: GPT-class models for summarization, Q&A, code, chat — via managed API with content filters.

example.code:
LANGUAGE PICKER:
  Analyze reviews → Sentiment (Language service)
  Translate docs → Translator
  Voice assistant → Speech service
  Chatbot/summarize → Azure OpenAI
example.walkthrough: Azure OpenAI vs OpenAI API: Azure adds enterprise security, private networking, and regional compliance.

pitfalls: Sending PII to public AI APIs — use Azure OpenAI with data controls.
Expecting perfect translation — always human-review critical content.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick the service: support ticket sentiment, multilingual manual, meeting transcription.

lessons.title: Generative AI & Prompts
concepts: Generative AI creates new content: text (GPT), images (DALL-E), code (Copilot) — trained on vast data, predicts likely outputs.
Prompts steer the model: clear instructions + context + examples = better output. Few-shot = examples in the prompt.
Tokens: the billing unit — roughly 4 characters per token. Long prompts cost more.
Hallucination: models can generate plausible-but-false content. Mitigate with grounding (RAG) and human review.

example.code:
PROMPT RECIPE:
  Role: 'You are a support analyst...'
  Task: 'Summarize this ticket in 3 bullets...'
  Context: paste the ticket
  Format: 'Bullets, under 50 words'
example.walkthrough: Never present AI output as verified fact — the exam tests hallucination awareness.

pitfalls: Trusting outputs blindly — hallucination is a top exam topic.
Ignoring token costs — long contexts get expensive fast.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write a prompt that summarizes a paragraph in one sentence. Count roughly the tokens.

lessons.title: Responsible AI Principles
concepts: Microsoft's six principles: fairness, reliability & safety, privacy & security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability.
Fairness: models must not discriminate — test across demographic groups.
Transparency: document what the model does and its limits (model cards).
Accountability: humans remain responsible — AI suggests, people decide.

example.code:
THE SIX:
  Fairness | Reliability & Safety | Privacy & Security
  Inclusiveness | Transparency | Accountability
  Mnemonic: 'Fair Reliable Private Inclusive Transparent Accountable'
example.walkthrough: AI-900 devotes real weight to Responsible AI — memorize all six with one example each.

pitfalls: Treating Responsible AI as fluff — it is scored content.
Deploying facial recognition without approval — restricted for a reason.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: For each principle, write one real-world violation example.

lessons.title: Relational Data: Tables, Keys, SQL
concepts: Relational data: structured tables with rows and columns; schema enforced. Think orders, customers, products.
Primary key uniquely identifies a row; foreign key links to another table's primary key — relationships without duplication.
Normalization reduces redundancy (split into related tables); denormalization speeds reads (fewer joins).
Azure SQL Database: managed relational PaaS — automated backups, patching, scaling.

example.code:
KEY VOCAB:
  Primary key → unique row ID
  Foreign key → link to another table
  JOIN → combine on keys
  Index → speeds lookups, slows writes
example.walkthrough: DP-900 tests normalization concepts and 'which database for structured data' picks.

pitfalls: Storing the same customer name in 50 order rows — normalize it.
No indexes on a million-row lookup table — full scans on every query.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Sketch orders + customers tables with keys. Write the JOIN to list orders with customer names.

lessons.title: Non-Relational Data: NoSQL Options
concepts: Document: JSON-like records (Cosmos DB, MongoDB API) — flexible schema per item.
Key-value: ultra-fast lookups by key (Redis cache) — sessions, counters.
Column-family: wide rows for time-series (Cassandra API) — IoT telemetry.
Graph: nodes + relationships (Gremlin API) — fraud rings, recommendations.

example.code:
NOSQL PICKER:
  Flexible JSON docs? → Document
  Blazing key lookups? → Key-value
  Time-series wide rows? → Column-family
  Relationships first? → Graph
example.walkthrough: Cosmos DB offers all four APIs — the exam asks which API for which pattern.

pitfalls: Forcing relational schema on semi-structured data — migrations on every new field.
Graph queries in SQL — recursive joins are painful; use Gremlin.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick the model: product catalog (varied attributes), session store, fraud network.

lessons.title: Data Ingestion & Processing: Batch vs Stream
concepts: Batch: process data in chunks on a schedule (nightly ETL) — high throughput, minutes-to-hours latency.
Streaming: process events as they arrive (IoT, clickstreams) — seconds latency, always-on pipelines.
ETL: extract, transform, load — classic warehouse pattern. ELT: load raw first, transform in the warehouse (modern cloud).
Azure Data Factory orchestrates pipelines; Stream Analytics / Event Hubs handle real-time streams.

example.code:
BATCH vs STREAM:
  Nightly sales report? → Batch (Data Factory)
  Fraud alert in seconds? → Stream (Event Hubs + Stream Analytics)
  Transform before or after load? → ETL vs ELT
example.walkthrough: Latency requirement decides: seconds = stream, hours = batch.

pitfalls: Batch for fraud detection — the money is gone by morning.
Streaming for monthly reports — paying for latency you do not need.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify: dashboard refresh hourly, sensor alerts, quarterly financial close.

lessons.title: Analytics: Warehouses, Lakehouses, Power BI
concepts: Data warehouse (Synapse): structured, curated, SQL-optimized for BI queries.
Data lake (ADLS Gen2): raw storage for any data type — cheap, schema-on-read.
Lakehouse (Fabric/OneLake): lake economics + warehouse performance — one copy, many engines.
Power BI: visualization — connect to warehouse/lakehouse, build dashboards, share securely.

example.code:
ANALYTICS STACK:
  Raw → Data Lake (ADLS Gen2)
  Curated → Warehouse (Synapse) or Lakehouse
  Visual → Power BI dashboards
example.walkthrough: DP-900 asks 'which for raw vs curated vs visual' — memorize this stack.

pitfalls: Querying the raw lake with BI tools — slow and expensive; curate first.
No data governance — lakes become swamps without catalogs and access control.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Map a retail analytics flow: POS data → ? → ? → store manager dashboard.

lessons.title: Data Governance & Compliance Basics
concepts: Classify data: public, internal, confidential, restricted — controls follow classification.
Microsoft Purview: data catalog, lineage, and compliance across the estate.
Retention: keep data as long as needed (legal/ops), then delete — storage and liability both grow otherwise.
Exam angle: 'track where data came from' → lineage (Purview). 'Control who sees PII' → classification + access.

example.code:
GOVERNANCE CHECKLIST:
  □ Classify (what sensitivity?)
  □ Catalog (Purview — where is it?)
  □ Lineage (where did it come from?)
  □ Retention (how long? then delete)
example.walkthrough: Governance is the difference between a data asset and a data liability.

pitfalls: No classification — everything treated the same, PII exposed.
Infinite retention — legal risk and storage cost compound.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify your own data: list 5 datasets, assign sensitivity, set retention.

lessons.title: Zero Trust: Never Trust, Always Verify
concepts: Zero Trust: verify explicitly, least-privilege access, assume breach. No implicit trust by network location.
Verify explicitly: authenticate + authorize every request using identity, device, location, risk signals.
Least privilege: grant only the access needed, just-in-time where possible (PIM).
Assume breach: segment networks, encrypt everything, monitor as if attackers are already inside.

example.code:
ZERO TRUST TRIAD:
  1. Verify explicitly (who + what + risk?)
  2. Least privilege (minimum access, JIT)
  3. Assume breach (segment, encrypt, monitor)
example.walkthrough: SC-900's headline concept — expect multiple questions phrased as scenarios.

pitfalls: VPN = trusted network thinking — Zero Trust verifies regardless of network.
One-time verification — every request re-evaluated, continuously.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Explain Zero Trust to a colleague in 60 seconds using the triad.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID: Identity Platform
concepts: Entra ID (formerly Azure AD): cloud identity — SSO, MFA, Conditional Access, Identity Protection.
MFA: two+ verification methods — blocks 99%+ of identity attacks. Non-negotiable baseline.
Conditional Access: policy engine — IF (user, device, location, risk) THEN (allow, require MFA, block).
PIM (Privileged Identity Management): just-in-time admin elevation — no standing admin rights.

example.code:
IDENTITY STACK:
  SSO → one login, many apps
  MFA → prove it twice
  Conditional Access → policy decides
  PIM → admin only when needed
example.walkthrough: Conditional Access is 'if-this-then-that for identity' — the exam loves policy scenarios.

pitfalls: MFA for users but not admins — admins are the highest-value targets.
Standing Global Admin — use PIM; standing privilege is standing risk.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write a Conditional Access policy: block legacy auth, require MFA for admins, allow trusted locations.

lessons.title: Defender: XDR Protection
concepts: Microsoft Defender XDR: unified SecOps — endpoints, identity, email, apps, cloud in one incident view.
Defender for Endpoint: EDR — detect, investigate, respond on devices.
Defender for Cloud: CSPM + workload protection — secure score, just-in-time VM access.
Defender for Office 365: anti-phishing, Safe Links, Safe Attachments.

example.code:
DEFENDER MAP:
  Endpoint → devices (EDR)
  Office 365 → email/collab threats
  Cloud → posture + workload protection
  XDR → all signals, one incident
example.walkthrough: XDR = cross-domain correlation; EDR = endpoint only. The exam distinguishes them.

pitfalls: Treating antivirus as EDR — EDR investigates and responds, AV just blocks known bad.
Ignoring Secure Score — it prioritizes your hardening backlog.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Map: phishing email → which Defender? Ransomware on laptop → which? Exposed storage → which?

lessons.title: Sentinel: SIEM + SOAR
concepts: Microsoft Sentinel: cloud SIEM — collect logs from everything, detect with analytics rules + AI.
SOAR: automate response with playbooks (Logic Apps) — isolate host, disable user, open ticket, no human delay.
Incidents fuse related alerts into one investigation — analysts work cases, not alert floods.
Threat intelligence + UEBA: know attacker infrastructure, spot anomalous user behavior.

example.code:
SOC FLOW:
  Collect (connectors) → Detect (analytics rules)
  → Investigate (incident graph) → Respond (playbook automation)
example.walkthrough: SIEM = detect/investigate; SOAR = automate response. Sentinel does both.

pitfalls: SIEM without automation — analysts drown in alerts; playbooks are the force multiplier.
No data connectors — Sentinel is blind without log sources.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a playbook: impossible-travel alert → disable user → isolate device → notify SOC.

lessons.title: Compliance: Purview & Data Lifecycle
concepts: Microsoft Purview: compliance portal — DLP, retention, eDiscovery, insider risk, communication compliance.
DLP: prevent sensitive data from leaving (email, SharePoint, endpoints) — policy-based blocking/warnings.
Retention labels: keep required data, delete the rest automatically — legal hold overrides deletion.
Insider risk management: detect risky user activity (mass downloads before resignation) with privacy safeguards.

example.code:
COMPLIANCE TOOLKIT:
  DLP → stop leaks | Retention → keep/delete on schedule
  eDiscovery → legal search/hold | Insider risk → people-centric signals
example.walkthrough: SC-900 asks 'which Purview capability for X' — memorize the toolkit.

pitfalls: DLP without tuning — false positives train users to ignore warnings.
Infinite retention — liability grows; defensible deletion is a feature.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write a DLP rule in words: block credit-card numbers in outbound email with user warning.

lessons.title: Management Groups, Subscriptions & Resource Groups
concepts: Management groups: top-level containers for governance across subscriptions — apply Policy once, inherit everywhere.
Subscriptions: billing + access boundaries — separate by department, environment, or workload.
Resource groups: logical containers for a solution's resources — deploy, manage, and delete as a unit.
Hierarchy: Management groups → Subscriptions → Resource groups → Resources. Governance flows down.

example.code:
HIERARCHY:
  Mgmt groups (governance at scale)
   └ Subscriptions (billing boundary)
      └ Resource groups (lifecycle unit)
         └ Resources (VMs, storage...)
example.walkthrough: Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it — the exam's favorite 'clean up' answer.

pitfalls: One subscription for everything — no cost isolation, no blast-radius control.
Resource sprawl with no groups — undeletable, unmanageable.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Design the hierarchy for: prod, dev, finance dept, marketing dept.

lessons.title: Azure Policy & Resource Locks
concepts: Azure Policy: enforce rules — 'only deploy to East US', 'require tags', 'deny public storage'. Audit or deny non-compliance.
Initiatives bundle policies (e.g., 'PCI-DSS set') for one-click compliance baselines.
Resource locks: CanNotDelete / ReadOnly — prevent accidental deletion or changes on critical resources.
Policy evaluates at deploy-time and continuously — drift gets flagged or remediated.

example.code:
GOVERNANCE PAIR:
  Policy → 'you must comply' (rules)
  Locks → 'you cannot break this' (protection)
example.walkthrough: Policy denies the action; locks block even admins. Both appear in exam scenarios.

pitfalls: Policy without remediation — audit-only policies that nobody reads.
Locks on everything — ReadOnly locks break legitimate automation.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write two policies in words: allowed regions, required 'owner' tag.

lessons.title: Cost Management: Tools That Control the Bill
concepts: Cost Management + Billing: analyze spend, set budgets, configure alerts at 80%/100% thresholds.
Pricing calculator: estimate before deploying — model the architecture, see the monthly cost.
TCO calculator: compare on-premises vs Azure total cost — migration business cases.
Tags: the foundation — tag by owner/cost-center/environment or cost reports are meaningless.

example.code:
COST DISCIPLINE:
  1. Estimate (Pricing calculator)
  2. Tag everything (cost-center, env, owner)
  3. Budget + alerts (80/100%)
  4. Review weekly (Cost Management)
example.walkthrough: 'Unexpected bill' scenarios always trace to missing budgets/tags.

pitfalls: No tags — unattributable spend, unfixable.
No budget alerts — discovering overruns at invoice time.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Design a tagging scheme: which 4 tags are mandatory for every resource?

lessons.title: SLAs: Reading the Fine Print
concepts: SLA: Microsoft's uptime commitment per service — 99.9% to 99.99%+ depending on configuration.
Composite SLA: multiply component SLAs (two 99.9% services in series ≈ 99.8%). Design accordingly.
SLA credits: if Microsoft misses, you get service credits — you must claim them; not automatic refunds.
No SLA for free tiers — exam trap: free services carry no uptime commitment.

example.code:
COMPOSITE MATH:
  App (99.95%) + DB (99.99%) in series
  ≈ 0.9995 × 0.9999 = 99.94%
  Series multiplies DOWN — redundancy multiplies UP
example.walkthrough: The exam asks composite SLA math and 'which has no SLA' (free tier).

pitfalls: Assuming 99.9% per component means 99.9% overall — series multiplies down.
Expecting automatic refunds — credits require a claim.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compute composite SLA: web tier 99.95% + DB 99.9% in series. (≈99.85%)

lessons.title: Service Lifecycle: Preview, GA, Retirement
concepts: Preview: beta features — no SLA, not for production, feedback welcome.
General Availability (GA): production-ready, SLA-backed, supported.
Retirement: Microsoft announces deprecation with (usually) 12+ months notice — plan migrations.
Exam angle: 'can we run production on preview?' → No — no SLA.

example.code:
LIFECYCLE:
  Preview → GA → (years) → Retirement notice → Migrate
example.walkthrough: Preview = no SLA is a favorite exam trap.

pitfalls: Production on preview — an outage with no recourse.
Ignoring retirement notices — forced migration under deadline.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Your vendor announces a service retirement in 12 months. Draft the 4-quarter migration plan.

lessons.title: AZ-900 Objective Map: Describe Cloud Concepts (25–30%)
concepts: This objective covers cloud models, CapEx/OpEx, and cloud benefits — the highest-weight AZ-900 area.
Expect scenario questions: match the model (public/private/hybrid) and the financial model (CapEx/OpEx) to requirements.
Shared responsibility appears here and in security — know who owns what per service model.
Study method: for each concept, write one scenario where it is the deciding factor.

example.code:
OBJECTIVE CHECKLIST:
  □ Cloud models with examples
  □ CapEx vs OpEx math
  □ Benefits: HA, scalability, elasticity, agility, geo-distribution, DR
  □ IaaS/PaaS/SaaS + shared responsibility
example.walkthrough: This objective is ~1/4 of your score — master it first.

pitfalls: Skimming definitions — the exam tests application, not recitation.
Ignoring the percentages — weight your study time by objective weight.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Score yourself 1–5 on each checklist item. Below 4? Re-study today.

lessons.title: AZ-900 Objective Map: Architecture & Services (35–40%)
concepts: Largest AZ-900 objective: regions/zones, compute, networking, storage options.
For every service: what it is, when to use it, and its key limits.
The exam's favorite format: 'which service for this requirement' — practice the pickers.
Hands-on: deploy a VM, create storage, build a VNet in a free Azure account — 30 minutes of clicking beats hours of reading.

example.code:
SERVICE FLASHCARD FORMAT:
  Front: requirement ('global NoSQL, ms latency')
  Back: Cosmos DB + why
  Make 30 cards. Drill daily.
example.walkthrough: Free-tier hands-on is the fastest path to 'which service' mastery.

pitfalls: Learning services alphabetically — learn by use case instead.
No hands-on — the portal makes abstract services concrete.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Make 10 flashcards today in the format above. Drill them tomorrow.

lessons.title: AZ-900 Objective Map: Management & Governance (30–35%)
concepts: Covers subscriptions, management groups, Policy, RBAC, cost tools, SLAs, and service lifecycle.
RBAC: role-based access — Owner, Contributor, Reader + custom roles; least privilege always.
Know the cost tools cold: Pricing calculator (estimate), TCO calculator (compare), Cost Management (track).
SLA math and 'no SLA on free/preview' are guaranteed points — do not leave them.

example.code:
GOVERNANCE TRIAD:
  Organize → Mgmt groups, subscriptions, RGs
  Control → Policy, RBAC, locks
  Optimize → Cost Mgmt, tags, budgets
example.walkthrough: This objective is pure memorization + simple math — the easiest points on the exam.

pitfalls: Confusing RBAC with Conditional Access — RBAC = Azure resource access; CA = identity policy.
Skipping SLA math — free points.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compute: composite SLA of 99.9% × 99.95%. Then list the three cost tools with one-line purposes.

lessons.title: AZ-900 Practice: 20 Rapid-Fire Checks
concepts: Q1: IaaS example? → Azure VMs. Q2: No SLA? → Free tier / preview.
Q3: Private + public together? → Hybrid. Q4: Pay only for use? → Consumption/OpEx.
Q5: 99.99% downtime/year? → ~53 min. Q6: Who patches VM OS? → Customer.

lessons.title: AI-900 Objective Map: AI Workloads & Considerations
concepts: Covers ML types, AI workload examples, and Responsible AI principles — roughly a third of AI-900.
For each workload (vision, language, speech, generative): know the capability and the Azure service.
Responsible AI's six principles appear as scenario questions — memorize with examples.
Anomaly detection, knowledge mining: know what they do in one sentence each.

Skipping Responsible AI — scored, not fluff.

lessons.try_it: Write one-sentence descriptions for: anomaly detection, knowledge mining, conversational AI.

lessons.title: AI-900 Objective Map: ML Principles on Azure
concepts: ML Studio: no-code/low-code model building — designer drag-and-drop vs automated ML.
Features vs labels, training/validation/test splits, overfitting — the core vocabulary.
Regression vs classification vs clustering: match the problem type to the scenario.
Know when to use prebuilt AI services vs custom training — prebuilt wins unless requirements are unique.

ML DECISION:

  Unique data/need? → Custom (ML Studio / Custom Vision)
  No ML team? → Prebuilt or no-code
example.walkthrough: AI-900 rewards 'use the simplest sufficient service' thinking.

Confusing validation and test sets — validation tunes, test judges.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: For: receipt OCR, custom defect detection, churn prediction — prebuilt or custom? Why?

lessons.title: AI-900 Practice: 15 Rapid-Fire Checks
concepts: Q1: Labeled + categories? → Supervised classification. Q2: Six principles? → Fairness, reliability/safety, privacy/security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability.
Q3: Plausible false output? → Hallucination. Q4: Billing unit for GPT? → Tokens.

Q9: Chatbot backbone? → Azure OpenAI. Q10: Custom image classes? → Custom Vision.

Q13: Memorized training data? → Overfitting. Q14: Restricted face tech? → Approval required.

Ignoring the six principles — guaranteed questions.

lessons.title: AI-900 Responsible AI Scenarios
concepts: Fairness scenario: model performs worse for a demographic → fairness violation; fix with balanced data and testing.
Transparency scenario: 'why did it decide that?' → model cards, documentation of limits.
Privacy scenario: PII in training data → privacy & security principle; use Azure OpenAI data controls.
Accountability scenario: 'the AI decided' → humans remain accountable; AI assists, people decide.

example.code:
SCENARIO TEMPLATE:
  Symptom → Which principle? → What fix?

steps.explain: Accuracy on an undisclosed test set proves nothing about fairness. Training on historical hiring decisions risks baking past bias into the model — the first responsible-AI question is always: what did this model learn, and from whom?

Ship it — the model is just reflecting reality

evidence: Current plan: no mention of AI in the application process.

Only disclose if a candidate asks

simulations.brief: An impossible-travel alert fires: a finance user's account signed in from two countries six minutes apart. You have Entra sign-in logs, and the risky-sign-in Conditional Access policy is in report-only mode.
simulations.debrief: You ran the identity incident loop: verify the signal, contain the session, follow the IR plan, then close the gap with enforced Conditional Access and stronger MFA.

evidence:
02:11 EST  Columbus, OH   Success (MFA: SMS)
02:17 EST  Lagos, NG      Success (MFA: SMS)
Device: unrecognized, both sessions
steps.explain: Impossible travel plus an unrecognized device is the textbook account-takeover signal — and SMS MFA is phishable. Verify before assuming: revoke the sessions and require re-authentication now. You can apologize to a traveler, but you cannot un-exfiltrate data.
options: Treat the overseas session as compromised: revoke sessions and force re-authentication
Assume the user is traveling and close the alert
Wait for the user to report a problem
Block the entire country in the firewall

evidence:
SharePoint: Finance-Q3.xlsx, Payroll-Export.csv, Vendor-Wires.xlsx
Downloaded 02:14–02:16 EST by finance-02 (overseas session)
steps.explain: Containment is not the end — data may have left. Follow the incident response plan: preserve evidence, assess what was taken, and notify the right people in the right order. Company-wide emails and silent hope both make it worse.
options: Start incident response: contain, preserve logs, notify per the IR plan
Delete the files and hope they were not copied
Email the whole company about the breach immediately
Do nothing — the session is revoked
steps.symptom: The overseas session accessed finance SharePoint and downloaded three files before you revoked it.

evidence:
Policy 'Block risky sign-ins': report-only mode
MFA method: SMS for 80% of users
steps.explain: Report-only policies protect no one — enforce the risky-sign-in block and replace phishable SMS MFA with phishing-resistant methods. Zero Trust means verifying every sign-in by risk, not trusting the network or the password.
options: Enforce the risky-sign-in policy and move users to phishing-resistant MFA
Keep report-only — enforcement might annoy travelers
Ban all travel
Require password changes every 30 days
steps.symptom: The account is secured. Leadership asks: how do we stop the next one?

sections.heading: Azure Concepts
items: CapEx vs OpEx — cloud's consumption model shifts IT spend from CapEx (upfront hardware purchases) to OpEx (pay only for what you use), which is exactly why idle on-premises capacity is wasteful.
Cloud economics — hybrid cloud combines on-premises/private infrastructure with public cloud, keeping sensitive workloads local while bursting to the cloud.
Elasticity vs scalability — scalability is the capacity to handle growth, but elasticity specifically covers the automatic, temporary dimension.
Common trap — resource groups are just billing labels with no real effect.
Common trap — resource groups enforce naming standards.
Common trap — resource groups can only hold one resource type.
Common trap — availability zones add redundancy.

A resource group is a lifecycle and management boundary — delete it and every resource inside is deleted too. That's why teams organize groups by project or environment — so cleanup is one deliberate action, not an accident.

sections.heading: AI Fundamentals
items: AI vs ML vs deep learning — deep learning is the ML subset using multi-layer neural networks. The data is labeled (each row has the known sale price), and the goal is predicting a numeric value — textbook supervised learning, specifically regression.

Supervised learning — unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data; reinforcement learning learns from rewards over time. Machine learning is the AI subset where systems learn from data instead of explicit rules.
Regression — Regression would predict a number like a price; clustering works without labels.
Classification — Classification assigns each input to a discrete category (spam vs not spam) using labeled training data.
Common trap — deep learning is the broad field containing AI and machine learning.
Common trap — machine learning contains AI, which contains deep learning.
Common trap — speech recognition for the scans, knowledge mining for the emails.
Common trap — the user interface must support screen readers.

sections.heading: Data Fundamentals
items: Relational — Relational databases organize data into tables with fixed schemas, enforce relationships via keys, and query with SQL — ideal for transactional data like orders and customers where structure is stable and integrity matters.

Non-relational data — a data lake stores raw data in any format cheaply at scale; a data warehouse stores curated, structured data optimized for SQL analytics. ETL (extract, transform, load) cleans data before it lands — classic for warehouses with rigid schemas.
OLTP — OLTP systems handle many small, fast read/write transactions (checkout); OLAP systems run complex analytical queries over large historical datasets (quarterly reporting).
Common trap — a data warehouse with nightly batch loads.
Common trap — a data lake used directly by BI tools with no curation.
Common trap — a relational database with a fixed schema.
Common trap — checkout is OLAP; the report is OLTP.

sections.heading: Security Fundamentals
items: Zero Trust — Zero Trust assumes breach and verifies each request explicitly based on identity, device health, and context — 'never trust, always verify.' The old castle-and-moat model trusted the internal network, which is exactly what the attacker exploited.

Security principles — defense in depth layers security controls (physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data) so that if one layer fails, others still protect the asset. Sentinel is for security operations/SIEM on top of that data.
Shared responsibility — the more managed the service, the more Microsoft owns.
IaaS — IaaS (VMs) leaves the guest OS and apps to you; PaaS (SQL Database) moves the OS, patching, and high availability to Microsoft; you always own your data and identities.
Common trap — resource locks encrypt data at rest.
Common trap — a network security group rule alone.
Common trap — TLS encrypts data at rest.
Common trap — patching responsibility is decided per subscription by support ticket.

sections.heading: Pricing & SLAs
items: Pricing models — the Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of specific Azure services; Cost Management tracks actual spend afterward.

Reserved capacity — spot VMs use spare Azure capacity at steep discounts with the trade-off that they can be evicted with short notice. Reserved instances/capacity trade commitment (1 or 3 years) for deep discounts — ideal for predictable 24/7 workloads.

Spot VMs — are cheaper but can be evicted anytime, which suits interruptible batch jobs, not contracted steady workloads. Azure Advisor's Cost recommendations surface underutilized resources (low-CPU VMs, unattached disks) to cut waste.
TCO Calculator — the TCO Calculator models your current on-premises costs (hardware, power, labor) against projected Azure costs for a migration business case.

Common trap — gives optimization recommendations, not migration TCO.
Common trap — an Azure Policy that deletes VMs on weekends.
Common trap — sLAs don't combine; each stands alone.

Composite SLA for serial dependencies — is the product of the individual SLAs: 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%. Every dependency you add lowers overall availability — a key reason architects minimize critical-path dependencies and design for redundancy.

sections.heading: Governance
items: Management — Management groups sit above subscriptions in the hierarchy (root → groups → subscriptions → resource groups). Tags are key-value metadata on resources that Cost Management can group and filter by — the standard mechanism for chargeback/showback.

Governance hierarchy — microsoft Purview scans and catalogs data assets, classifies sensitive data (like PII), and tracks lineage — the governance answer to 'where is our sensitive data?' Sentinel hunts threats; Purview governs data.

RBAC vs Azure Policy — azure Policy governs resource compliance (rules resources must satisfy, like allowed SKUs or regions). Enforcing required tags with Azure Policy keeps the data clean as teams deploy.
Resource — Resource locks (CanNotDelete, ReadOnly) block delete/modify operations even for users with permission — they're the guardrail against accidents and rogue automation.
Common trap — putting all resources in one resource group.
Common trap — the first is a resource lock; the second is RBAC.
Common trap — a single Azure Policy assigned per VM.
Common trap — enabling diagnostic logs on every resource.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Azure Concepts: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one AI Fundamentals lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Data Fundamentals terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
